title: Initial rates for hydrogen peroxide and iodide

stimulus.title: Initial rates at 25 °C
stimulus.html:
In acidic solution, hydrogen peroxide oxidizes iodide ions: H₂O₂(aq) + 2 I⁻(aq) + 2 H⁺(aq) → I₂(aq) + 2 H₂O(l). Initial rates of formation of I₂ were measured at 25 °C.

Initial concentrations and initial rates
Trial[H₂O₂] (M)[I⁻] (M)[H⁺] (M)Initial rate (M/s)
10.100.100.101.20 × 10⁻⁴
20.200.100.102.40 × 10⁻⁴
30.100.300.103.60 × 10⁻⁴
40.100.100.201.20 × 10⁻⁴

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Determine the rate law for the reaction.

rubric.point: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]: doubling [H₂O₂] doubles the rate (trials 1, 2); tripling [I⁻] triples it (trials 1, 3); doubling [H⁺] has no effect (trials 1, 4)

parts.sample: Trials 1 and 2: [H₂O₂] doubles and the rate doubles, so first order in H₂O₂. Trials 1 and 3: [I⁻] triples and the rate triples, so first order in I⁻. Trials 1 and 4: [H⁺] doubles and the rate does not change, so zero order in H⁺. rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻].

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the value of the rate constant, k. Include units.

rubric.point: k = (1.20 × 10⁻⁴ M/s)/((0.10 M)(0.10 M)) = 1.2 × 10⁻² M⁻¹ s⁻¹, with correct units

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A student claims the reaction happens in one elementary step, exactly as the balanced equation is written. Explain why the data do not support this claim.

rubric.point: A single elementary step would give rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]²[H⁺]², which does not match the measured orders (first in I⁻, zero in H⁺); a five-particle collision is also extremely unlikely
accept: the orders do not match the coefficients, so it cannot be elementary

parts.sample: If the equation were one elementary step, its rate law would come from its coefficients: rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻]²[H⁺]². The data show first order in I⁻ and zero order in H⁺, so the reaction cannot be a single step. A collision of five particles at once would also be far too unlikely.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Trial 1 is repeated at 35 °C and the initial rate is larger. Explain this observation in terms of the collisions between reacting particles.

rubric.point: At higher temperature a larger fraction of collisions has energy at or above the activation energy (the energy distribution shifts higher), so more collisions are effective per second; the activation energy itself is unchanged
accept: more particles have at least Ea, so more successful collisions

parts.sample: At 35 °C the particles have a higher average kinetic energy, so the distribution of energies shifts to higher values and a larger fraction of H₂O₂–I⁻ collisions has at least the activation energy. More collisions per second are effective, so the rate (and k) is larger. The activation energy is the same at both temperatures.
